question: A junior doctor reads chest radiographs by looking first at the most obvious abnormality and then stopping. Which statement best explains why this approach is unreliable?

answers.text: The obvious abnormality may be normal variant, so it should be ignored on first pass.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Obvious abnormalities should not be ignored; however the problem with stopping after the first finding is that additional, clinically important abnormalities will be missed.

answers.text: Inexperienced doctors should not look at chest radiographs independently.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Developing the skill of systematic radiograph reading is an explicit MBBS competency. The issue is not who reads the film but how — without a systematic search pattern, findings are missed.

answers.text: A systematic search pattern ensures every anatomical region is examined, preventing satisfaction-of-search errors that cause additional findings to be missed.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. 'Satisfaction of search' is a well-documented perceptual error — once a finding is spotted, the observer stops searching and misses co-existing pathology. A memorised, systematic search pattern applied to every film prevents this by ensuring exhaustive coverage.

answers.text: Radiographs must always be read in the radiology department to be reliable.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Clinicians are expected to read radiographs at the bedside and in casualty. The key is applying a disciplined systematic method, not the location of the reading.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the section on why a disciplined normal-radiograph template is the first interpretation skill. The satisfaction-of-search error is the main hazard of non-systematic reading.
Correct. A systematic search pattern prevents satisfaction-of-search errors and ensures every region is examined.
